title: The bramble king (Judges 9:7–15)
hookLine: Jotham's fable: olive, fig and vine refuse to rule; only the bramble wants to

cards: A voice shouts down from the top of Mount Gerizim to the city of Shechem below. It's Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon, alive because he hid.
His half-brother Abimelech has just murdered the rest of the brothers, and the men of Shechem have made Abimelech king. Jotham can't fight him. So he tells them a story about trees.
Hearken unto me, he calls down, that God may hearken unto you.

teach.h: OLIVE, FIG AND VINE SAY NO.
teach.b: Once, the trees went out to anoint a king. They asked the olive: reign over us. Should I give up my oil, it said, that honors God and people, to go and sway over the trees?
They asked the fig. Should I give up my sweetness and my good fruit? They asked the vine.
Should I give up my wine, that cheers God and people? Each has real work to do, and won't trade it for a crown. Last, they go to the bramble, a low thorny bush with no fruit worth picking.
And the bramble says yes. Come and take shelter in my shade. Some readers smile at that: a bramble has almost no shade to give.

Then, in the same breath, a threat: "and if not, let fire come out of the bramble, and devour the cedars of Lebanon." So the fable says two things. The ones with something to give were too busy giving it.
The one with nothing to give wanted the crown most, and promised shelter while warning of fire. Jotham turns it on Shechem: if you've dealt honestly with my father's house, enjoy your king.
If not, let fire come out of Abimelech and burn you, and fire come out of you and burn him. Then he runs.
In the end, Shechem and Abimelech turn on each other and both are destroyed, and the text says the curse of Jotham came upon them.

how: Jews study Jotham's fable in Judges 9 as part of the Former Prophets; it is often read alongside Gideon's refusal of kingship in Judges 8 when teachers discuss power and leadership.

o: a fruit vine too proud to give up its wine
a low thorny bush with no fruit, eager to be king
a tall cedar of Lebanon that shaded every tree

games.q: the bramble wants the crown — tap the pairs.

s: the olive, the fig and the vine all refused to be king
each would not give up its own gift to sway over the trees.
Jotham told his fable to the trees of Lebanon
he shouted it from the top of Mount Gerizim to the men of Shechem.
Jotham's curse on Shechem and Abimelech came true
by the end of Judges 9, the two sides have destroyed each other.

games.q: you're the olive tree. all the trees come to you and say: reign over us. what do you say?
o: should I give up my oil, that honors God and people, to sway over the trees?
only if the fig agrees too.
games.why: the olive says no, and so do the fig and the vine. only the bramble says yes, and it threatens fire if it isn't obeyed.

practice: Bring to mind one group you belong to, a family, a team, a group chat, and notice, without judging anyone, who quietly bears fruit there and who wants the crown.
Then turn it gently on yourself: where are you the olive tree, and where are you the bramble?

wordCard.voice: bramble. The low thorny bush in Jotham's fable, the only tree with nothing to give that still said yes to the crown.

orig.note: Hebrew: a thornbush, the bramble that wants to be king in Jotham's fable.

carryVoice: Your line: the bramble wants the crown. The olive was too busy giving oil. That's day seven hundred twenty.
